# The Long Walk Home

Lily had taken the shortcut through Mr. Patterson's field a hundred times. The wooden fence at the back of the property was old and weathered, the top rail worn smooth from years of kids climbing over it. At thirteen, she was tall enough now to vault it in one motion, the way her older brother did.

That afternoon, she was running late for dinner. Her mother had warned her about cutting through the field in her good Sunday dress—the pale yellow one with the white collar—but Lily was sure she could make it home before anyone noticed.

She placed her hands on the top rail, swung her legs up and over, and felt the world go wrong.

There was a sharp tearing sound, loud and final, followed by a tug that yanked her sideways. She landed hard on the grass on the other side of the fence, the breath knocked out of her. For a moment, she just lay there, staring at the cloudy sky.

Then she sat up.

Her dress was gone. Not entirely—the fabric was still there, hanging in tatters from a rusted nail that jutted out from the fence post like a crooked finger. The whole back of her dress had ripped away, and what remained was hanging by threads at her shoulders. When she tried to gather it around herself, the fabric simply came apart in her hands like wet paper.

Lily's face went hot. Then cold. Then hot again.

She was crouched in the grass behind the fence, in nothing but her underclothes, and her house was still half a mile away across open ground. The road ran along the edge of the field. Anyone driving past would see her. Anyone walking by would see her.

She pulled her knees up to her chest and tried to think. Tears welled up, blurring everything. She couldn't go forward. She couldn't go back. She couldn't even stand up without exposing herself to the whole world.

"Stupid, stupid, stupid," she whispered, pressing her forehead against her knees. Mama had told her. Mama had told her not to wear the Sunday dress, not to take the shortcut, not to climb the fence. And now here she was, half-naked in a field, and any minute someone was going to come along and *see* her, and she would die. She would just die of it.

She heard footsteps in the gravel along the road.

Lily curled herself into the tightest ball she could manage, hiding her face. *Please keep walking,* she prayed. *Please don't look this way. Please, please, please.*

The footsteps slowed. Then stopped.

"You alright over there?"

It was an old voice, gravelly. She recognized it before she dared to peek—Mr. Hollis, who lived in the little white house at the end of her road. He had to be seventy at least. He waved at her sometimes when she walked to school.

She couldn't answer. Her throat had closed up entirely. She just shook her head, still pressed against her knees, her ears burning so hot she thought they might actually catch fire.

She heard him take a few steps closer, then stop. There was a long pause. He must have seen the dress hanging on the fence. He must have understood.

"Ah," he said softly. "I see."

She wanted to disappear. She wanted the ground to open up and swallow her whole. She would have given anything—*anything*—to not be there in that moment.

"Now listen, young lady," Mr. Hollis said, and his voice was kind but matter-of-fact, the way a doctor's voice is. "I'm going to set my jacket down on the grass right here by the fence, and then I'm going to walk on down the road a ways and look at the sky. You come get it whenever you're ready. Alright?"

She managed a tiny nod, though she didn't think he could see it.

She heard the soft sound of fabric on grass. Then his footsteps moved away, crunching steadily down the gravel until they were distant.

Lily lifted her head just enough to peek. There, draped over the fence rail, was a brown canvas work jacket, old and softened with years of wear. Mr. Hollis was a good twenty yards down the road, his back to her, hands in his pockets, looking up at the clouds as if he'd never seen anything so interesting.

She bolted for the jacket. It was huge on her, falling almost to her knees, and it smelled like pipe tobacco and hay. She wrapped it tight around herself and buttoned every button with shaking fingers. Even covered, even safe, her face was still burning. She didn't think it would ever stop burning.

"Thank you," she called out, her voice small and cracked.

Mr. Hollis didn't turn around. He just raised one hand in a wave. "You get on home now," he called back. "And tell your mama I said hello. Don't worry about the jacket—bring it by whenever."

Lily ran.

She ran the whole half mile home, the jacket flapping around her legs, and she didn't stop until she was through her own back door. Her mother took one look at her—at the enormous brown coat, at her tear-streaked face, at the absence of any dress beneath—and didn't say a single word about the Sunday dress. She just opened her arms.

A week later, Lily walked the jacket back to Mr. Hollis's house, freshly laundered and folded neatly. Her mother had baked a loaf of banana bread to send along with it. Lily set both on his porch, knocked, and—because she still couldn't quite bear to look him in the eye—hurried back down the steps before he could answer the door.

But she waved at him after that, every time she passed. And he always waved back, like nothing had ever happened at all.
